channel.title: Technology Reading
channel.description: Articles about software, publishing and the open web.

item.title: Matt Mullenweg returns as Automattic CEO after two-day ouster
item.description: Matt Mullenweg says he is back as Automattic CEO only two days after its board placed him on paid leave. WordPress executive director Mary Hubbard confirmed his return, while The Verge reports CFO and brief interim CEO Mark Davies lost Slack access. The unusually public boardroom fight matters to WordPress, Tumblr, WooCommerce, Pocket Casts and the broader open-source web.

item.title: Former Climate.gov staff rebuild its public mission on the open web
item.description: Three former NOAA staffers have rebuilt Climate.gov's public-facing mission at nonprofit Climate.us after the federal site was dismantled in 2025. The team restored archives, hosts vanished resources such as the Fifth National Climate Assessment and raised $530,000 to keep accessible climate reporting and data on the web.

item.title: Static ActivityPub publishing takes an RSS-like approach
item.description: Evan Prodromou demonstrates a read-only ActivityPub model that works more like RSS: static files that other servers poll, without queues, signatures or fanout. His FEP-b06c profile, Jekyll plugin and GitHub Pages demo aim to make federated publishing practical for independent sites and small developers.

item.title: Current turns RSS reading into a river instead of an inbox
item.description: Current rethinks RSS as a river instead of an inbox: items fade on schedules matched to their type, while readers can tune source speed, mute noisy feeds, follow individual voices and import OPML. The $9.99 Apple app has no subscription, and a web version is planned.

item.title: WordPress launches a private site creator that runs in a browser
item.description: WordPress.org's my.WordPress.net creates private sites entirely in a browser, with no account, host or domain. Built on WordPress Playground, it stores data locally and supports experiments with themes, plugins, drafts and a personal RSS reader.

item.title: The Ankler moves from Substack to Ben Thompson's Passport
item.description: The Ankler is moving its publishing operation from Substack to Passport, a subscription platform from independent publisher Ben Thompson built with Automattic. Axios reports the move will give the outlet more control over its audience, data, bundles, podcasts and events while it keeps a smaller Substack presence.
